subject: Estimating birth cohort differences using tests linked by anchor items and respondents

messages.author: 900cd0718d2352a1
messages.subject: Estimating birth cohort differences using tests linked by anchor items and respondents
parts:
I want to estimate whether there are significant changes in the subject matter competence of Norwegian pupils across birth cohorts using a large sample of standardized tests built around an anchor design.

In attempting to answer this question using mirt, I have two questions:

1. How can I get standard errors for the estimated cohort-specific means (relative to the first cohort scale that was standardized to mean 0 and standard deviation 1)?
2. The results using only anchor pupils and anchor items gives results consistent with what I have found using other approaches, but the results using all pupils and all items gives bizarre and non-credible results. Am I doing something wrong in the function call for multiGroup in this instance?

Background and data description: Norwegian 5th and 8th grade students in Norway answer a standardized test in three different subjects every year. The tests are developed using IRT methodology, and each year a random sample of pupils (~3500 out of a total of ~60 000) have a portion of the test replaced with a set of "anchor items" used to link the tests and ensure that the scale is comparable across years. The anchor items are re-used annually (but gradually renewed over the years by replacing older items with new ones).

The data I have access to are anonymized, with a line for each pupil and a column for each question. The columns are named for the question they represent, and the question-names (a numeric code) is fixed for each item. Anchor items can thus be identified as questions posed repeatedly across multiple years, and anchor pupils can be identified as pupils answering multiple anchor questions.

Viewing the anchor items and ignoring the cohort-specific items, I set up a dataset with one column for each anchor question and one line for each anchor pupil, along with a variable for which birth cohort each child (i.e. data row) belongs to. I also create a vector (named item_type) for the items as some of them are polytomous - with binary items assigned "2PL" and polytomous items "gpcm". The first line of the data gives the test year, while the remaining columns give the scores for the individual anchor items.

As I understand the documentation, the invariances I want to impose are slopes and intercepts (since the groups are years, and the assumption of the anchoring procedure is that the item parameters of the anchor items are the same over time), but also "free_means" and "free_variance" (as both the mean and the variance of later birth cohorts could differ from the first birth cohort.

I thus specify the model as
    multi_year_irt <- multipleGroup(anchor_pupil_data[, 2:length(colnames(anchor_pupil_data))],
                                     model = 1,
                                     method = "EM",
                                     itemtype = item_type,
                                     group = paste0("cohort_",year_group_key[anchor_pupil_data[, 1]]$year),
                                     invariance = c("slopes", "intercepts", "free_means", "free_variance"))
                                     
 Having run the model, I extract the group means using the coef function, e.g., the cohort mean for the 2015 cohort is found as coef(multi_year_test,
                    simplify = T)$cohort_2015$means
                   
 The first question is how I get standard errors for these means?
 
 The second question concerns the effects of including all the data (all pupils, all items from all years of a specific combination of grade-level and subject, e.g. 8th grade english). Since the cohort-specific items are cohort-specific, the assumed invariance for slopes and intercepts across groups should not matter for these items: they are only observed for one cohort each. I thus ran the same specification, merely replacing the data with one that included all items ever used in the test and all the test data from all the pupils (anchor pupils and others) in all birth cohorts. Items not assigned and answered by a pupil were given missing values (NA).
 
 My expectation was that the anchor items would be handled "automatically" as they appear in different birth cohorts and the invariance imposes the same slopes and intercepts for items appearing in multiple groups. I also expected that the trends in group means (i.e., birth cohort means) would change slightly but stay more or less the same. I expected small changes since the anchor pupils are randomly drawn and may differ from the rest of their birth cohort due to sampling variation. By including all pupils, I expected that any random sampling variation making the anchor pupils in a year more or less representative would be corrected for. For instance: if the anchor pupils in a year on average had below-average competence in a subject, this would be apparent from their responses to the cohort-specific questions they had answered and the way these compared to the non-anchor pupils' responses to these same items. Instead, the results showed a massive and implausible shift from cohort 1 to cohort 2 (more than one standard deviation - e.g., a shift of more than 1), followed by much smaller changes.
 
 Is there some problem with using the above function call to estimate the birth cohort means using all the data at the same time - do I need to more explicitly inform the model about the structure of the data (who is anchor pupils and what items are anchor items)? Are there issues when using large amounts of data (a single analysis would now have about 470 000 pupils, each answering a subset of about 400 total items used in the test across all years)? (The convergence alghorithm stopped after 500 iterations - should I boost this number and see if that helps?)

Sincerely,

Ole Rogeberg

messages.subject: Re: Estimating birth cohort differences using tests linked by anchor items and respondents
parts:
Update: Here is a figure  that further suggests that the mirt produces odd results when using all the pupils (whether or not they answered the anchor items) and all items (anchor and non-anchor): the trends produced depend strongly on the specific years included.

The curve shows the estimated trend in cohort means for two subject-grades, each estimated four  times using different subsets of the data. I use the same function call as before for both, and use data for all students (anchor and non-anchor) and all items (anchor and cohort-specific items).To compare estimated trends, the series that drop years at the beginning of the period are aligned with one of the longer curves at this point.

As you can tell from the plot, the curves deviate substantively - and in implausible ways.
